utterances.text: You weren't able to hear their -- any noise coming from anywhere within the hangar building at night-time.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that one could hear before I fell asleep was people talking, and I mean -- I don't know how to explain it. I couldn't -- I couldn't hear any -- practically any major -- now, how shall I explain it to you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. We can move on. From -- the detainees that you saw in the hangar building, did you -- did you notice any bruising on their bodies?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't see anyone bloodied or anything. There were no visible marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many toilets are there in the hangar building, if you know?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hangar -- well, once again, I can't be precise. I should say that there were -- first there were wash basins with the taps, and I think there were about five or six on one side and on the other sinks with faucets. And I'm sure that there were five or six WC cubicles and at least six male urinaries, but perhaps -- urinals. But I didn't count them. Perhaps there were more. I've been thousands of times there. But one can check it easily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were there, between -- I'm interested in the period May to August -- end of May to August. What were the conditions of these toilets?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, conditions weren't really particularly hygienic. Many people came there. There was a sanitation service which put chlorine in there and there was a water hose and one could wash it. But to tell you the truth, it wasn't all that clean. But considering that it was wartime, I'd say it was accessible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, though, that those toilets were clogged up very, very early on and these were the toilets that these one to two thousand detainees had to use?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really definitely say that nothing was clogged or anything, but there was water and there was a hose and one could wash it. But there was also another toilet in the building up here. I mean, in the administrative building on the lower level. There were also toilets here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move now to another topic. In relation to the food, it's the case, isn't it, that you didn't either cook or distribute the food?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was no cook. I was an electrician. I didn't distribute food. But I was in the kitchen. I was -- I went to the kitchen in order to maintain, repair, be it refrigerators, or the heating installations, lights, so that I saw the food being repaired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were the meals taken over to the cafeteria once they were cooked? Were all the meals taken over at one time?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is something that I can't really -- I know that food was transported. Whether it was all done in one go or in two or how many, I don't know that. But be that as it may, the food was taken over. Perhaps it also depended on the kind of vehicle. There were small vehicles. There were bigger vehicles. I don't know how -- so I can't tell you really whether it would all be taken in one go or on two occasions. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the food being put onto a truck?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, food was carried over, and I think it was a small truck. Naturally, nobody carried it on his back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a TAM truck?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a small truck. We all called it TAMIC, little TAM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that could be marked as S15-41, which I think is the next number in the bundle of photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please be so kind and confirm that 41 would be the next one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then provisionally marked S15-41.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the photograph in front of you, was that the sort of truck that was used to transport the food?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this one, this couldn't be that one, because this one doesn't have wheels, does it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's true. It doesn't have wheels now. But it did have wheels certainly in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I object to the form of the question, Your Honour. Because this picture certainly doesn't depict the vehicle as it looks "now," and counsel should, for the record, at least tell us when the picture was taken. We certainly know it wasn't taken today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First, sustained. Second, I think we can read it from the picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just about to give the source of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the date also is readable.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. This photograph was taken in February 1996 within the Omarska mine by members of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you have identified that as a truck that was used to transport the food; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with that photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Are you able to read the registration number on that truck?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if this was exactly this one. I can see the registration plate. There were several such vehicles. There was not just one of them. Because there were several vehicles in the mine across various parts of the company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the audio-visual director please zoom in on the number plate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to read the number plate now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You can zoom out a little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it read "PD 545-46"?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this registration plate has been changed. I don't recall this registration plate. This registration plate existed before the war, and then during the war or after the war they were replaced by the Cyrillic ones. Whether these registration plates were used during the war, I haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with that photograph. Could the witness please be shown S379.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the meantime, objections against the admission into evidence of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, S15-41.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you take a moment to read that short document. Have you read the document?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated in your testimony yesterday on page 70 other people who had worked at the mines who were then given a work obligation to work at the camp. I want to take you through this document and I want you to tell the Court -- if we go to part 2, the permanent shift employees in the iron ore mine, if you recall what their duties were in the mine. So if we can start with the first name, Dusko Vlacina.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I start answering?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusko Vlacina was some sort of a manager or director, a technical director.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing after the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He was not in Omarska. He was in Prijedor in the main administration. I believe that he was a member of the management. I believe that he was a technical director. But I can't be sure. In any case, he was in Prijedor together with Nedeljko Vujicic, Branko Drljic -- I don't know Branko Drljic. Milorad Serdar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you can pause there. I want to do this systematically and I want you to go through those persons listed under the "Permanent shift employees," and I want you to tell the Court those names of the people you knew and what obligation they had from the end of May 1992 and only those names of the people that you remember that were working there and the duty that they had. I don't want to know what position they held when they worked in the mine prior to their work obligation. Sir, as you go down that list, do you know the person mentioned at number 2, what his duties were -- what his work obligation duties in the mine were?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what his duties were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 3?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drljic -- Branko Drljic. I don't remember this man at all, Branko Drljic. It is possible that he worked in the separation plant. He did -- in the pit where I was, what could he be doing there? He may have been in the separation plant. Maybe something to do with the water pumps. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe we can move this along a little faster. Can you point to the people -- can you name the number of -- and the name of the people that were drivers.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kicema Branko, Milorad Stakic were drivers. But again, a problem. We all call him Mico. But maybe in the books he's recorded as Milorad. That may be the same person. I don't know. I've never inspected his ID card, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've just told us about numbers 10 and 11. Is there anyone else listed that you recall being a driver?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was Pero -- driver Pero, but he is not on the list here. Pero ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about number 17, Vlado Kobas? Was he a driver?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado Kobas was a locksmith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was prior to his work obligation. Do you recall what he was doing on his work obligation?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under his work obligation, he was in the workshop all the time doing some welding. I think that from time to time he also drove, but he is not a driver by profession. He didn't work as a driver in the mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Omarska trial, when you testified, you mentioned three drivers of TAM trucks. And this is for Trial Chamber and Defence at page 4769 [sic]. You mentioned Mico Stakic, a person called Pero Mrdja, and Vlado Kobas as being drivers of TAM trucks. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the transcript maybe it's a mistake. It reads "4769." I think you make reference to "7469."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that testimony in the Omarska trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would just object to the form of the question again, Your Honour, and based on the Court's prior ruling I would just respectfully request that counsel puts the specific question and the answer given as previously so that the witness can answer the question without any mischaracterisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that I'm not mischaracterising any evidence, I will take you back a question or two. Question: "What was done with the bodies that you saw lying inside the Omarska camp? You've told us that you saw bodies I think on more than one occasion. What was done with those bodies?" You answered: "They were taken away somewhere. I didn't take them. I don't know. How should I know? I was doing my job. I had nothing to do with that." Question: "Who took those bodies away?" Answer: "There were people who transported them. I was not authorised to drive them off or anything else." Question: "Who transported the bodies away from the camp? Who drove them off?" And you answered: "There were drivers. Mico Stakic and Pero Mrdja. Vlado Kobas was also a driver. He drove the vehicle. But who actually drove, I don't know. I didn't see that." "What sort of vehicle was used to take the dead bodies out of Omarska camp?" You answered: "The mine had a small vehicle which we called a TAMIC. It was a TAM van, yellow. All the mines' vehicle were yellow. And the workshop had that particular vehicle at its disposal for its affairs around the compound."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would respectfully request, so that it's placed in its proper context, the next two questions and the next two responses be read for the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next question was: "How many times did you see bodies being transported in that yellow TAM truck?" Answer: "I did not see that at all." Question: "How do you know that the bodies were taken away in the TAM truck? That's what you just testified to." And you answered: "As the vehicle existed, that was the only vehicle that existed, so nobody could have carried the bodies on their backs." Sir, do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that testimony, but I did not see the vehicle that took the bodies away. Maybe the police came or the military. I know that there was this particular vehicle in the workshop, but I didn't see it taking the bodies away. Maybe a military team came or a police team came for the purpose of taking the bodies away. I don't know. I do not claim that it was this precise vehicle. What I said was that that vehicle was at the disposal of the workshop. For instance, when I had to go to the well, which is 5 or 6 kilometres away, or to the separation plant, which was 2 kilometres away, it brought in food. I didn't see who was it who collected the bodies and who took them away. Maybe it was the military with a military vehicle or the police with a police vehicle. I didn't see it. I'm not claiming that it was the truck belonging to the mine that took the bodies away. It could have easily been another vehicle that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is related to the drivers, not -- at this point I don't want to talk about the dead bodies being taken away from the camp. I simply want to know whether there's anybody else besides three persons that you mentioned when you testified in the Omarska trial, that is, Mico Stakic, Pero Mrdja, and Vlado Kobas that you remember as being drivers of the trucks, the TAM trucks?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the mine was still operating, there were a few more drivers. But I don't think that they were there when -- let me see if Branko Kicema is still here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned him. He's listed at number 10. What I'm interested in is --

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at this document, S379, are there any other names listed between numbers 1 and 28 in part 2 that were drivers as part of their work obligation from the end of May until at least the end of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drivers -- drivers were Branko Kicema, Milorad Stakic, Pero Mrdja, but Pero Mrdja is not on the list. Those were people who were drivers. And there were probably other people who could drive. So whether any of them drove, despite the fact that they were not drivers -- maybe somebody else who was not a driver could have taken a vehicle, because they could simply drive. They knew how to drive. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in relation to Pero Mrdja, did you know this person?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was a driver employed by the mine. He worked in the mine as a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I may have confused you. I meant did you know him personally? Do you know whether he's related at all to Dragan Mrdja?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether they are related. I know the guy worked with me for six or seven years. Who is he related to, I haven't a clue. I know he lives in Prijedor. I don't know his address, but I know that he lives in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I misspoke. I meant to say Darko Mrdja.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who he is related to. I just know the guy from the mine from the time when we worked together. Who his relatives are, I really haven't the faintest idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you were driving around the mine to the well and to the pumps, did you drive the TAM truck or did someone else drive for you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was usually driven by Pero Mrdja. I believe that we were usually on the same shift, that he was in my shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the spring and summer of 1992, fuel was a precious commodity, was it not?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was more expensive than gold itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And TAM trucks, they ran on diesel fuel?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that you could travel approximately 100 kilometres on 15 litres of fuel, 15 litres of diesel?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me object to the form of question. I think, Your Honour -- although counsel may be an expert in terms of fuel consumption. It obviously makes a difference on the weight and other factors that can contribute to the consumption of fuel, whether it's diesel or gas. I guess that would be my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objection dismissed. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer my question. Do you agree that you could travel on 15 litres of diesel approximately 100 kilometres or so?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't drive, and I didn't watch the consumption. It depends on the type of vehicle. Do you mean the TAM vehicle?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a normal average TAM truck.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the horsepower. I can't tell you, because there are bigger lorry, smaller lorries, all sorts of lorries. It depends on what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, the TAM truck shown in photograph S15-41.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really never put fuel in it. I never drove it. I didn't measure the consumption. It may be possible, but no, I can't give you any answer. I can't say either yes or no. I really never drove that type of a lorry. I never put any fuel in it. I never measured the consumption of that lorry. I never tested it for its consumption. I really cannot give you any answer. I can't say either yes or no, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time. It's 5.30. Would you like to take a break now, or may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown a bundle of one exhibit with a number of pages within it, which is a new exhibit. And for the Trial Chamber's and Defence's benefit, these documents were seized by the OTP from the second floor of the Separacija office building, the Omarska iron ore mine on the 26th of February, 1996. Your Honour, there are 14 reports within that one exhibit, and if it could be marked as Prosecution Exhibit S395, I think is the next number. Copies were provided to the Chamber and Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear. What is the ERN number of the first page? Because I can't see any?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Down at the very bottom, Your Honour, 00381813.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That is also the number of the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will read the 14 ERN numbers so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay..

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So the second one -- sorry, the first one is dated the 2nd of June, 1992. The ERN number 00381813. The second one is dated the 4th of June, 1992, ERN 00381826. The next is dated the 6th of June, 1992, ERN 00381774. The next one is dated the 7th of June, ERN 00381850. The next, the 9th of June, 1992, ERN 00381840. The next, 10th of June, 1992, 00381865. The next, 11th of June, 1992, 00382907. Next, 12th of June, 1992, 00382917. The next is the 15th of June, 1992, 00382949. The next is the 16th of June, ERN 00381776. The next is the 18th of June, 1992, 00381732.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Doesn't it read "18th of July, 1992"?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we provided Your Honours and counsel with these -- with two additional pages. I'm taking them in chronological order. If you take these two pages from the registrar, the two pages she has in her hand. So chronologically after the 16th of June, we have the 18th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: ERN 00381732. The next, 19th of June, 1992, ERN 00381731. Next, 18th of July, 1992, ERN 00382961. And finally, the 19th and 20th of July, 1992, ERN 00382962. Your Honours, we have provided an English translation only of the first page, which sets out the headings of the document, and they are reports on the fuel quantities received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If there is no protest, Madam Registrar, it would be provisionally marked as S395; correct? So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so it's clear, the Defence does have an objection to the document, Your Honour, and we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the moment, it's only provisionally marked, as usual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you take a moment to look through those documents.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise these documents?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why one truck would in a 12-day period, that is, from the 2nd of June to the 19th of June, over 12 days, do you know why they would consume over 477 litres of fuel?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. Perhaps they were engaged in contraband. It was very expensive, so perhaps they were selling it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or perhaps they were transporting bodies from the Omarska camp to other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll object to the form of the question. It calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, looking at these documents, you have stated yourself that a number of the drivers -- earlier in your testimony you mentioned, for instance, Branko Kicema, Vlado Kobas, and Milorad Stakic. Do you see their names within these documents -- and Pero Mrdja?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see -- I see Vlado Kobas. Let me see. Branko Kicema, Vlado Kobas, Vlado Kobas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So looking at the first document, the 2nd of June, we can see that Branko Kicema was driving TAM truck PD 545-46, which is the same TAM truck in the photograph that you saw earlier, S15-41, is it not?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go to the next document, the 4th of June, we can see Branko Kicema again driving PD 545-46. We also see Vlado Kobas driving a TAM truck PD 641-58. The next date, the 6th of June, Vlado Kobas again driving TAM truck PD 545-46. Looking alone at PD 545-46, we can see that it goes through 477 litres of diesel in that 12-day period at the beginning of June. You mentioned that these were drivers from the Omarska mine. Do you know what they would be doing to drive that many miles in those days?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me object to the form of the question and also object to the mischaracterisation as to the number of days between the documents and to counsel' calculation. In addition to those two objections, I would object that the question has already been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be better you had included three different questions in one. So if you could have a breakdown question by question and then it would be maybe easier for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true the mine wasn't operating during this period of time and that there was no -- there was --

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no, no. No, no, no. Of course it was not working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore, the only activities that these TAM trucks and other vehicles would have been used for was in relation to the Omarska mine, the camp -- the Omarska camp, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we have here is a pure and simple theft of oil, and people were selling it. They would get it. They would be issued with it, and then they would either sell it to somebody or use it for their own tractors, because at that time a litre of oil was 5 marks. 400 litres is a lot of money, and that's the game we have to talk about, not something else. But they covered it with these papers, saying that yes, so much fuel was issued for that -- such and such vehicle. For instance, we have here Milorad Vuleta, he got this diesel for his tractor, which has nothing to do with the -- with the camp. Because there was all fuel in the camp and then everybody tried to get for his own purposes this. I mean, that was what it was, theft of fuel, nothing else but.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was referring to the drivers that you had mentioned as being drivers in the Omarska camp while it was operational. Sir, at the time the mine wasn't functioning, who would have approved the use of fuel which you say was more expensive than gold?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat when and who approved. During the camp time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When the mine wasn't functioning, who would have approved the use of fuel?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody approved anything. Whoever managed to tank it did that. I'm not aware of anyone issuing any orders. I saw people coming in their tractors to petrol stations, simply filling in their tanks and leaving because there was nobody there. What we are talking here about is theft, pure and simple, and contraband in fuel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you to make a clear distinction between that what you know and what is your speculation, please. A short time ago you told us that you have never seen the papers -- these papers. And later on, page 42, line -- where is it? -- Line 15, "They covered it with these papers." So if you haven't seen these papers before, I think would it be correct to assess this would -- it's speculation, or do you have any indicia or even evidence that at that time petrol was in fact stolen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never saw these documents prior to this day. But I'm quite sure that this is fuel contraband. No need for any further -- no doubt about it. For instance, fuel was received by people who were never -- I don't know, Kobas, BMW, I don't know. I mean it wasn't my job, and I don't know who issued fuel, when issued fuel. I was busy. I have no idea about any fuel, when, who issued it, how issued it. Who used it up, when. That is something I don't know. But if you ask me something about electrical engineering and high voltage, I'd be able to answer that. But as for the fuel, I haven't the slightest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the place where bodies have been exhumed from, Kevljani, how far is that from the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Kevljani. I've never been to Kevljani. How far is it? Well, I can make another guess and we can haggle as on the green market, but I've never been there. I don't know. Could be more than 10 kilometres. I don't know. I have no idea. I really cannot answer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Today's transcript, page 12, line 21 you testified on the question, "There no beds at all, no." How is it possible that you can come to this conclusion or to this testimony? Did you visit all the buildings and all the rooms in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? May I start talking? In the beginning, when the camp started, there were no beds at all. I spotted -- I started spotting some beds in the latter half of August. I remember how the troops, the military, brought in some beds, but I didn't have one. And in the early days, there were no beds at all, and we saw that throughout the period. I was speaking only -- I was referring only to the early days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have free access to all rooms in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't have free access everywhere. I only worked in those areas which were of vital importance as regards things electric. In rooms where there were no important electric installations, I never went into them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown document S15-17. Have you ever seen such a room with such a number of beds and mattresses?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a room in the administrative building, I think on the ground floor. But I didn't go in there. I saw the troops bring beds only once, but that was sometime I'd say in the latter half of August. Before that, there were no beds whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you actually ever see detainees sleeping on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in beds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. Just -- your testimony was that beds were brought only later. But, say, in the period end of May, June, July, did you ever see inmates lying on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The inmates were on the floor, yes, until -- until those beds were brought in the second half of August. In the beginning, yes, they were on the floor. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And could you please give us a description what was the space available for one person in this room.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't do that, not in detail. But I know it was crowded. I know they had very little room. I think they had to be -- to lie one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you see children there?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't see children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you see women there?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were several women, and I came to know the mother of a fellow worker of mine. She washed dishes in the cafeteria where the food was distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why was it that she was detained there?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss with your colleague about this?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I talked with my colleague who worked with me -- I mean, he was under the same conditions, I mean, under the detention conditions, and his mother was also there, and they went to see his mother and we talked, that her son was there, that he was all right, that nobody was harming him, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that all, call it, staff members, opposed to detainees, were specially marked? Wearing, for example, some special insignia or something else that there could be a clear distinction made between inmates, investigators, typists, and so on?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. The difference between inmates and investigators? Were they differently marked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For example, you -- I think you mentioned already previously how was it possible to identify you as being not an inmate in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. I was marked. Yes, I did have this white armband. And we who were under work obligation, we all had those white armbands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it only those people under work obligation wearing these white armbands or also other persons working there, maybe in the kitchen, maybe as investigator, maybe as typist?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not notice the typists or other personnel, investigators, that they had anything. No, I don't think they had any -- any markings to distinguish them, as far as I can remember, because I never went into the rooms occupied by investigators. I could see them only when they came in the morning, on a bus, get off the bus, and enter the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know Ms. Markovska?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Markovska, no, I did not come to meet her during the camp. I met her here in 2001, when we came here to testify in Mr. Kvocka's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you meet her later again?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss with her the testimony?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't. No, no, I did not see her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You met her, but you didn't see her. In 2001. The question was -- you answered, on page 47, line 13, "I met her here in 2001." My question was whether or not you at that time only met her or had a discussion with her.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only met here at the time of the testimony in Mr. Kvocka's case. We did not discuss anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's return to Omarska. Were there special rooms for the detention of women?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether there were any special rooms, but I used to see women in the restaurant washing dishes, and they were in the administrative building. Whether there was a special room assigned for them, I do not know. I did not go there, so I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were there any prohibited area where you weren't allowed to enter into?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, access to the white house was prohibited for me, and I couldn't really go -- go everywhere. I had certain itineries which were safe, because there were also minefields around, and just because of my safety I wasn't really particularly eager on going everywhere, and I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why was it that there were minefields around?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were minefields behind the police in a ring which was held by the army. I don't have a sketch to explain it. Perhaps some 150 metres away from the buildings, behind the buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown document S15-2 another time. Could you please indicate where these minefields were.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't show it here, because we see only the end of the asphalted area of the pista, and the minefields were down there. There's a petrol station down to the south, and they were behind that petrol station, and then to the north, because there is where Bare is, where meadows are, and there were trenches which were held by the army, and that is where the minefields were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: These minefields, had they been there before May 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No, they were laid when the inmates arrived, because in those early days, in the beginning -- at the beginning there was -- there were power cuts and there was chaos, so that later on I had to put up a generator -- a power generator here in front of this administrative building, and I had to put up the flashlights at these two corners to light the area, because in the early days there were even some attempts at escape and fire was opened. That is what I heard, because I wasn't there. I mean, I didn't really see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown once again S15-2-2. If you could be so kind and take once again the marker and mark those places where you had to put up the flashlights.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I also mark where the power generator was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could be so kind and mark the two flashlights with "3" and "4." Because we had already 1 and 2, and now 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And in which direction headed these flashlights?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their lights were directed westward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So that they would cover the so-called pista, the area between the two buildings; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We called it flower bed because here were flower pots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would be correct that your testimony is that the flashlights had the purpose to lighten the area between the two buildings? Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. When there was no electricity, then I would switch on the power generator so as to be able to see the entrance into the building and this area here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, you testified - it's quite clear that you can't tell us now whether it was the 23rd, 27th, 30th of May - but how many days after your beginning with your work under the work obligation in this area did you build up these flashlights?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't give you the precise date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it before the detainees arrived or after?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was after the arrival, maybe five or four days after the arrival. Again, I can't give you a precise answer. I can't tell you what date it was, how many days later. I know that people were already there. There were very frequent power cuts. It would be dark in the evening, and that's when we put the power generator here and connected lights to that generator and we also conducted electricity to the administrative building where the typists were and where the investigators were so that they could do their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I then ask the usher to take my own copy of document S15-16 and this be marked in addition with a "-1." And could you please indicate with the marker where the aforementioned -- where the aforementioned minefields were located. I think the other way around.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you can't see the petrol station at all, but this is on the southern side, so thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the other areas you mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is here that I noticed them, but I believe that they were also here on this side, across the road, somewhere around here. Or maybe even here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You didn't make use of your marker. Could you please make use of this marker and indicate that we can follow -- at least on my PC I can't see it. This one I can see, yes. And then where else?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And who told you and cautioned you and warned you that there were these minefields in order to protect your life and limb?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was warned by the army, because I would come from my house from this direction here, from the west, and that's why I would always go in the morning when it was already daylight. I avoided going during the night. I was afraid that I might get killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were there armed policemen protecting these buildings?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. But they were around the buildings, around the white house, and they were in front of the administrative building, and here in the southern part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... these places were to the best of your recollection, these -- I don't know whether it was police, army -- these armed persons were with a "P."

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be your testimony that on the other side of the hangar there was no armed police or army patrol?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was behind this part, behind the petrol station. The petrol station is somewhere here. But in any case, there were guards all around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Armed guards.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why was it that you weren't allowed to enter the white house?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It must have been an order by the police. I don't know. In any case, I didn't need to go in there. I didn't want to go in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The final area I want to cover is the following: How many delegations to the best of your recollection ever visited Omarska during, say, end of May until September 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember two delegations. The first one was the one that came in luxurious cars, and the second delegation was in the second part of August. And those were foreign journalists. I don't remember the date again, but in any case they arrived as you can see here in front of the administrative building. This is where they stopped. They were escorted by the police, and I was here at the end of this big building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness pointed to the area where he himself marked a "P" in front of the administrative building for the area where the journalists were, and he indicated that at that point in time he was in front of the right-hand side of the hangar. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Relatively far away. Did the journalists have --

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did the journalists have access to all the buildings?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see, I recognised them as being journalists. They had cameras. They entered the administrative building as far as I could see. This is where they walked. And later on I don't know where they went. I went into the workshop. It was very hot. I was tired, so I went take a rest. They took some photos. What photos they took, I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's come back to the first delegation. I think your testimony was extremely clear where this delegation arrived. And is it correct that your testimony is that the delegation came with two cars?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, those were two luxurious passenger cars. And as far as I can remember, one of those was a Mercedes and the other one was a Golf, if my memory serves me right. Again, I cannot guarantee that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The two drivers remained in the car; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And wasn't it your testimony that seven or eight persons completed this delegation? Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember. I did not count them, and I didn't make a note of that, so I don't know whether there were seven or eight, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I haven't the transcript before me, unfortunately. Could you please repeat the names of those persons you recall having seen there.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew - and I will repeat - the president of Banja Luka municipality Predrag Radic, then Simo Drljaca and Simo Miskovic. These were the people I knew. I didn't know the others. They had armed escorts with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you estimate how many armed escorts had they with them?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, there were two or three of them. Again, I can't remember that precisely. It was a long time ago. It was 11 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you said "seven to eight persons," these two to three were already included, or were they additional persons protecting the delegation?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were with the delegation, so I counted them in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Predrag Radic. How did you know this person? From television, from radio, from former visits to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Predrag Radic from before the war. He was a very successful businessman. I even saw him in Banja Luka in the street. I saw him in the papers. And that's how I was able to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca, I knew him because I would see him in the camp rather often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why was it that Mr. Drljaca often visited the camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was -- I don't know what he was by his position. I know he was the chief of the Secretariat of the Interior. I only know that I used to see him there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the term "Crisis Staff"?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you know if so that Mr. Drljaca was at that time a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the people were in the Crisis Staff. I only knew that the Crisis Staff existed. That's what I heard. I don't know who was in it, how it was, who had what position in it. I really don't know. I was not into any political matters at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was it from the municipality of Prijedor and the person who was in charge of taking care about what happened in Omarska that you, for example, received the necessary material that Omarska was provided with the necessary or after following your testimony sometimes even unnecessary fuel and all these daily necessities for to run Omarska?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please ask that question again. I'm not sure that I understood you correctly. So would you please be so kind to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there any person, if any, from the municipality of Prijedor taking care of the, say, hygienic situation, the -- as it was your field where you were working in, the electricity, that you had the necessary material and so on -- a person responsible for the running of Omarska, that everything worked as foreseen?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was any such person. I only know that Simo Drljaca was there, that he could issue orders to people there. And I don't know anything else. I don't know. I really don't know who it could have been. Only Mirko Babic or the management of the mine could give me orders, and for the rest I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who gave you, for example, the order to put up these flashlights?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mirko Babic, the manager of the workshop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And in hierarchy, who would be able to order Mr. Mirko Babic to act or not to act?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There was a chain of command in the mine, in the mine structure. There was, for example, the manager. Above him was the director. I am not familiar with the functioning of those structures. I don't know what their sequence or order was. In any case, I received orders from Mirko. Mirko received -- or may have received orders from the director of the mine. And that was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it is your testimony that the director of the mine was, also at that time, when the mine as such was no longer operational, was in the -- in this hierarchy, that he had some say in Omarska? Is it really your testimony?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that he could do things that had to do with the mine, with the processes in the mine, when something needed to be done in the mine. There was the management of the mine and the management of the mine could order things to be done. Nobody else could give me the order to go and repair the electrical facilities. For example, nobody from the police or the army could order me to go and repair the well. It was only the management structure of the mine who could do that, the manager of the workshop or whoever. And I believe that he took his orders from a higher position, that is, from the director of the mine, that he was the one who could order him. That was my understanding of how things were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be more concrete, was there a kind of separation of powers, one restricted to the running of the mine and one limited to the responsibility vis-a-vis the detainees, or was there an overlapping responsibility?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the mine did not have any authority over the detainees, that it was up to the military and the police to do that, and that the mine did not have anything to do with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you have identified Mr. Kovacevic if he would have been part of this delegation?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know Dr. Kovacevic. I didn't know him. Only now I can see his photo in the hospital. Before that I didn't know him and I was never in the hospital and -- no, I wouldn't recognise him, because I didn't know him at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you know at that time Mr. Brdjanin, if he would have been part of the delegation, would you have seen him?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At the time I didn't know Mr. Brdjanin. But now if I could go back to those times -- I don't know. I can't -- I don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I see that you try hard to memorise that what happened ten years ago, Mr. Vuleta. But can you tell me -- can you be quite sure that in fact you saw the entire delegation, or may it be that part of a delegation was separate and the cars not entering the area as such?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I saw the entire delegation. I saw them coming from the direction of east and I saw them stopping where they stopped. I have already told you that they passed by me, that they went behind the restaurant and they were westbound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Correct. You testified previously only briefly that you heard the persons, the detainees, singing -- I believe you said "Serb songs." What kind of songs were these?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were Serb songs. One of them is "Who says that Serbia is little? Who lies that Serbia is little?" Then from "Topola to Radana Gora." Then there was a song Vojvoda Sindjelic, and other Serbian songs. I can't remember all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When did this singing start?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The singing started when the cars stopped there and when the delegation passed by me and went in the direction of the west.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be your testimony that in advance there was no singing at all?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. There may have been. It's very difficult to say one or the other. They may have been singing even before that or they may have started when they arrived. I didn't pay too much attention to that. I was thinking about repairing the damage to the electrical line. I didn't even try to memorise the sequence of these events. I only remember that I heard the songs being sung.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But wasn't it your testimony that you surrounded the entire area in order to identify the place where this technical problem was at that time, and when surrounding this entire area, no doubt before you found this mistake and you repaired this, didn't you hear at that time already singing of Serbian or Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Like I've told you, I'm not sure. Maybe I did. Maybe they had been singing. I didn't have a tape recorder to record that. I just remember that I heard the singing. At the moment when they arrived, there was singing to be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The detainees, were they lined up? And if so, where?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The detainees were lined up in front -- I don't have it in front of me to show it to you. They were lined up in front of the administrative building and in the area on the eastern side, to the east of that big building and on the southern side of this huge hole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the model -- on the picture we have before us, on the side of the administrative building where we don't have the restaurant, on the other side, and in addition to the left-hand side of the hangar; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the south side of the administrative building; on the eastern side of the big building of the hangar, and partly on one side of the big hangar building, if I'm make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the delegation of high-ranking persons, did they pass these lined-up inmates singing Serb songs?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived from Omarska, from the direction of the east, and they arrived in the eastern side of the administrative building. That's where the cars stopped. High-ranking officials got off the cars. The drivers had remained behind. The officials went towards the rest, towards the northern part of the restaurant, and from there on I couldn't see them because I did what I told you I did; I wanted to finish that job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, can you tell me the ethnicity of the Omarska camp population.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Omarska camp, there were Muslims and Croats. There were even some Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Were your acquaintances or friends detained in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were my fellow workers, my electricians, those who used to work with me in the same mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And why they were detained?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, they were detained because an attack had taken place on an army column coming from Banja Luka somewhere. I'm not quite sure where. Jakupovic, somewhere. Some part of Kozarac at any rate. And they attacked the army there, and I heard that they had killed two soldiers there. And after that, the attack on Prijedor followed and fighting started there, and then naturally the army surrounded it and those people were brought there in order to establish who had been those extremists, who had attacked the army, who had organised the attacks, to investigate that and naturally to then let honest people go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did your acquaintances who were detained in the camp participate in the attack on Hambarine or Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not. And those guys are still alive today, and they always greet me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have no more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I don't have any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence. How many questions do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This concludes your testimony. We're grateful that you came to The Hague and that you testified, that you gave us your view and your memory. And it's extremely important to hear both sides, and therefore thank you and we all wish you a safe trip home. Thank you. May the -- may I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for listening to my story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it remains for us to decide on the admission of evidence. This would be S15-2-2. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's the case. Admitted into evidence as such. Then -- I have lost the overview. If you could help me, please, S15 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections? If not the case, admitted into evidence as such.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And S395, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections? The bundle of paper, put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to S15-16-1. But 395 was the Prosecution exhibit, so Mr. -- Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. It's only for Mr. Ostojic. Please, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We do have an objection to that document. As the Court duly noted on page 57, line 16 of today's transcript, my learned friend specifically said that these documents were seized on February 26, 1996. The Defence would like a couple of questions answered in connection with that seizure. First of all, was it consistent with the rules and was it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you slow down, Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. Thank you. First of all, was it issued pursuant to the rules as the proper subpoenas in another seizure was indicated or was it also a unilateral attempt by the Prosecutor to seize documents? Secondly, the Defence is enormously concerned that these documents were not tendered in advance and they do not bear a 65 ter number pursuant to the Rules. Third -- there's a couple more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Let's come back to the question of 65 ter numeration in connection with the three other documents we still have to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. I'd just like, if I can, on this third one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The third point, if the Court notes that the picture that the Defence -- or strike that. The picture that the OTP utilises, specifically S15-41 was shown that to this witness and produced to this witness, and we had an objection as to the date of that exhibit. It was clear that that tram, according to the OTP's testimony or statements, I should say, that that document was photographed on February 23rd, 1996. So the Defence is very curious to know how is it that they subpoena documents three days' prior, yet were allegedly on the premises of the iron ore mine taking photographs or pictures. And we'd like a clarity on that. And we think that it's an important issue. Finally, with respect to Exhibit 3 -- S395, the Court will note that some documents have signatures on the sixth column of the documents. Other documents and the predominant number of documents within Exhibit S395 do not bear those signatures. We're perplexed as to how these things continually and consistently happen. We have other concerns in connection with these documents but we raise those four at the present time for the Court. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In line with the Rules and the guidelines on the admission of evidence and for the reason that the witness testified on the basis of these pieces of paper, to put it this way, this bundle of documents is admitted into evidence. The English one and single page translated S395A, and the B/C/S bundle S359B-1, 2, and forth following, please. We have to return to the question of 65 ter documents later. I recall Mr. Lukic asked for the discussion in the presence of Mr. Ostojic. Are there any urgent matters to be discussed today? I know it's extremely difficult for the Defence to prepare a proffer for Monday. The number of the witnesses we can expect for Monday would be, question mark?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is -- it is a question mark, Your Honour. But we'll attempt tomorrow night, as we have in the past, to e-mail to the OTP and to the Chamber a copy of the proffer of the witness, and at the latest, I would suggest that by 11.00 Sunday morning so that they would have enough time. And I know it may be inconvenient for the Court since we do convene early next week, but we will provide the OTP with the amended proffer and we'll endeavour to do the same with the Court. Because I do believe we have the e-mail of the proper Court personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you have already the numbers and your 65 ter number of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're not sure, because tomorrow they're arriving. But I did list four of them, and we're just not sure of the order yet until we meet with them tomorrow. We anticipate that it may be 053, but we're not sure until we meet with him and then we'll make that decision. And again, it involves scheduling for later in the week. This witness may be lengthy, so we want to just make sure to put him in the proper category so that he could finish his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We will prepare for 053, and it may be -- create problems for us if another witness goes ahead of 053.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So may I invite the parties to concentrate on S -- the yes. What was it? S53, that we all can try to prepare this together for Monday. And please do the possible. I know it's extremely difficult for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We appreciate that. And we'll tell them immediately once we make that decision. So if he's prepared today -- I mean, tomorrow within 14 or 18 hours, he'll know exactly the one. But again, because of the schedule, we'd just like to reserve that right. And we'll try bring him if he's ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I can't see any additional urgent matters. I thank all participants, and I apologise for once again, especially on a Friday afternoon or evening, to have some overtime. But it enabled the witness to leave The Hague and stay during the weekend in his home country. I thank all of you, especially the interpreters giving access to the testimony of the witnesses. The trial stays adjourned until Monday, 9.00, in this courtroom. And I wish a very good weekend for everybody.
